newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil gov't sees no signs of overheating economy.
newsitem.headline: Brazil gov't sees no signs of overheating economy.

text.p: The Brazilian government sees no signs of an overheating economy, saying industrial production growth in second half 1996 is running behind the expansion rate of the second half of 1994, the Finance Ministry said.

In its monthly report on economic indicators, the ministry said the recovery had been gradual and differed from sector to sector, while incomes were not growing at an accelerated rate and there were signs insolvency was on the rise.
"The evolution of economic activity in the last few months does not suggest the Brazilian economy is on a path of excessive recovery," the report said.

The report said industrial expansion was "significantly" lower than in the same period in 1994, when a consumer boom spurred the government to tighten credit and implement other monetary restrictions in early 1995.
It said industrial production in December 1994 expanded 15 percent from June that year while industrial production in September 1996 was up just 8.0 percent on January this year.
The ministry said gradual income growth would naturally limit the rate of economic expansion this year as new consumers paid off recently-assumed obligations.
"Insolvency could show some increase again in the next months due to seasonal factors, which will contribute to a natural slowing-down of economic acticity at the start of 1997," the ministry said.
"The future outlook suggests a process of gradual recovery without the risk of the economy overheating," it concluded.

The markets have been buzzing with speculation that early 1997 could see a repeat of early 1995's credit clampdown after Brazil posted 7.0 percent gross domestic product growth in the third quarter of 1996 compared with the same year-ago period.

Imports have also surged, resulting in a $2.9 billion trade deficit for the year so far and prompting the government to deny repeatedly that it plans to revert to "stop-and-go" economic policies to dampen demand next year.
